# How to Earn Enough Points for a Free Flight


A one-way award flight can start at **4,500 points** . That is the published starting rate for short-haul economy awards in[Atmos Rewards](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) , the Alaska Airlines program formerly called Mileage Plan.


Most people searching for how to get free flights assume that to earn enough points for a free flight you need six figures. That assumption is the reason they never start.


The bigger surprise: about three in four general purpose credit cards in the U.S. are now rewards cards, and consumers earned more than $40 billion in rewards in a single year, up over 50 percent from 2019 ([CFPB](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_credit-card-rewards_issue-spotlight_2024-05.pdf) ). If you hold one of those cards, you are already earning. You have just never aimed it at anything.


This guide is about getting the points. Finding and booking the seat is a separate job, and our guide on[how to book flights with credit card points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-book-flights-with-credit-card-points) covers that end. This one stops where that one starts.


You will get what a real trip costs in points, the three ways points come in, how long ordinary spending takes, and what to do when you get there. At Pointhound we search 21 loyalty programs and 200+ airlines across 75,000+ routes, so the prices below come from what award seats cost, not from a brochure.


*Advertiser disclosure: Pointhound earns affiliate commissions on some credit cards. Card details here were taken directly from the issuers' own pages and verified on August 14, 2026. Welcome offers change often and vary by applicant, so confirm current terms with the issuer before you apply.*


## How Many Points Do You Actually Need for a Free Flight?


A one-way award flight starts around 4,500 points for short domestic routes, roughly 12,500 for Hawaii, and from about 6,000 to 40,000 for Europe.


Start with the destination, not the method. Most beginner guides explain what points are and then tell you to go earn some, without ever naming the target. If you do not know what the trip costs, you cannot judge whether any of this is worth the effort.


Trip Typical one-way points Roughly what that seat sells for in cash Full guide


Short domestic economy, under 700 miles From 4,500 $100 to $250 Covered below


Hawaii economy from the West Coast From 10,000 to 12,500 $300 to $600 \[Flying to Hawaii with points\](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-fly-to-hawaii-with-points)


Europe economy From 6,000 on the cheapest program, more typically 20,000 to 40,000 $600 to $1,200 \[Flying to Europe with points\](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-fly-to-europe-with-points-complete-guide)


Wherever points stretch furthest right now Varies by month Varies \[Where your points go furthest\](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/where-your-points-go-furthest-award-flight-deals)


The 4,500 figure is the[Atmos Rewards](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) starting rate for routes under 700 miles. Hawaii economy from the West Coast starts at 10,000 or 12,500 points each way depending on the airports ([The Points Guy](https://thepointsguy.com/loyalty-programs/points-and-miles-to-hawaii/) ). Europe has the widest spread: Virgin Atlantic Flying Club lists one-way transatlantic economy from 6,000 points, while most programs land between 22,500 and 40,000 ([Upgraded Points](https://upgradedpoints.com/travel/best-ways-to-fly-to-europe-with-points/) ). Air France-KLM Flying Blue prices standard economy to Europe at 25,000 miles one-way and runs monthly Promo Rewards from 18,750 ([The Points Guy](https://thepointsguy.com/loyalty-programs/ultimate-guide-flying-blue/) ).


Cash figures above are typical economy fares for these routes, not quotes for specific dates. The point costs are starting prices on good days, not fixed rates. Award pricing moves with demand and programs revise their charts, which Atmos states on the chart itself:


> "Actual redemption rate requirements may vary based on route-specific factors, including city pair combinations, partner airline pricing, market demand, number of flight segments in the itinerary and limited availability at lower tiers."


**"Free flight" is shorthand.** The real term is *award flight* : a seat bought with points instead of cash. Points cover the fare, but taxes and carrier fees still appear at checkout. On Atmos that means a $20 partner award fee per person each way on partner bookings. Flying Blue adds carrier-imposed surcharges on top, and those climb in premium cabins. A few dollars on some programs, several hundred on others. Beginners rarely hear this before their first booking, which is why the checkout total comes as a shock.


## Where Do Credit Card Points Come From? The Three Ways to Earn


Points come from three places: a welcome bonus for opening a card, everyday spending on that card, and smaller extras like shopping portals, referrals, and flying.


The internet calls this travel hacking, which makes it sound like a trick you have to be clever to pull off. It is not. It is putting spending you were already doing on a card that pays you in points instead of nothing.


Earn path Typical size How fast What it requires


Welcome bonus 75,000 points on the two cards below About 3 months A card application, a credit check, and a minimum spending requirement


Everyday spending 1 to 5 points per dollar Continuous, forever Moving spending you already do onto the card and paying it off in full


Portals, referrals, authorized users, flying A few hundred to a few thousand at a time Occasional A few extra steps, and someone to refer


**1. The welcome bonus.** A *welcome bonus* is the lump sum an issuer pays you for opening a card and spending a set amount within a set window. It is the largest single deposit most people will ever receive. The[Chase Sapphire Preferred](https://creditcards.chase.com/rewards-credit-cards/sapphire/preferred) is currently offering 75,000 points after $5,000 in purchases in the first 3 months. The[Capital One Venture](https://www.capitalone.com/credit-cards/venture/) is offering 75,000 miles after $4,000 in the first 3 months. Both carry a $95 annual fee. One bonus that size already covers several of the trips in the table above, with points to spare.


**2. Everyday spending.** Cards pay a base rate on everything and a higher rate in specific *bonus categories* , meaning types of spending the issuer chooses to reward more, like restaurants or travel.


Sapphire Preferred earns 5 points per dollar through Chase Travel, 3 on dining, 2 on other travel, and 1 on everything else. Venture takes the opposite approach: a flat 2 miles per dollar on every purchase, with 5 on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel. Category cards reward concentrated spending, flat-rate cards reward spending that is spread out, and neither approach is wrong.


**3. Everything else.** Shopping portals pay extra points when you start an online purchase from the issuer's own shopping site. Referral bonuses pay you for referring someone who gets approved. Adding an authorized user sometimes pays a small bonus, and flying earns miles directly with the airline. Worth knowing as a beginner: award bookings can sometimes earn miles too, depending on the program, so a points ticket is not always a dead end.


None of this works if the card carries a balance. Interest costs more than the points are worth, every time. If you are not paying in full each month, points are the wrong project. For the fundamentals before the tactics,[Points 101](https://www.pointhound.com/points101) is the shortest version.


## Sign-Up Bonuses vs Everyday Spending: Which Gets You There Faster?


A welcome bonus delivers in months what everyday spending takes years to build, but it pays once per card and requires hitting a spending minimum.


Do the arithmetic in the open, because it settles the question fast.


A 75,000-point welcome bonus arrives after roughly three months, once you have spent $5,000 on the Sapphire Preferred or $4,000 on the Venture. Now earn the same 75,000 points through spending alone at Venture's flat 2 miles per dollar. That takes $37,500 of purchases. For a household spending near the national average of $78,535 a year across everything, housing included ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cesan.nr0.htm) ), $37,500 on one card is a year and a half of disciplined routing, not a quarter.


So the answer is not "which one," it is "in what order." **The bonus is the accelerator. Everyday spending is the engine that keeps running after the accelerator is spent.** Most people need both, because a bonus fires once per card and then never again.


One caution the card-recommendation sites tend to bury: a minimum spending requirement is only worth chasing with spending you were going to do anyway. Buying things you do not need, or paying fees to route money through a card, cancels out the value of the bonus and then some. If the $4,000 is already going to leave your account over the next three months, the bonus is close to free. If it is not, the math stops working.


Both offers above were checked with the issuers on August 14, 2026. Welcome offers change constantly and vary by applicant, and both issuers restrict eligibility if you have held the card or taken its bonus before. Treat any bonus figure you read anywhere, including here, as a current offer rather than a standing fact.


## How Long Does It Take to Earn Enough Points for a Free Flight?


It depends on your spending and whether you open a new card, but a first short-haul award flight is commonly a matter of months.


This is the question every beginner has, and few guides answer it. Here is an answer, with the assumptions on the table where you can change them.


Each scenario assumes four things: the spending goes on one card, the balance gets paid in full every month, the earn rate is the one listed, and no points are spent along the way. The spending figures are anchored to real household data. U.S. households spent an average of $78,535 in 2024, including $10,169 on food and $13,318 on transportation ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cesan.nr0.htm) , released December 19, 2025). Food and transportation together run about $1,960 a month, and those are the categories that reliably go on a card. Housing usually does not.


Scenario Assumed monthly card spend Earn rate used Points after 12 months What that range covers


Modest spender, card you already hold $800 ~1.3 per dollar blended (3x dining, 1x rest) About 12,500 A couple of short domestic one-ways, or one one-way to Hawaii


Average spender, card you already hold $2,000 2 per dollar flat About 48,000 Round-trip Hawaii, or a one-way to Europe with room left


Average spender who opens one card and earns the bonus $2,000 2 per dollar plus a 75,000 welcome bonus About 123,000 Round-trip economy to Europe for two, at typical transatlantic pricing


The blended 1.3 rate in row one comes from applying a 3x-dining, 1x-everything card to the spending mix the BLS figures imply. Change the inputs and the answer changes with them: spend more and every row shortens, hold a flat 2x card and row one nearly doubles, skip the new card and row three disappears.


This table is an illustration built on stated assumptions, not a prediction about your account. Your spending, your card, your issuer's current offer, and award pricing on your dates will all move the answer, and award prices themselves change month to month.


For most beginners the first award flight is much closer than they assumed, and the first business class seat is much further. Row one reaches Hawaii inside a year on ordinary spending. None of these rows reaches a lie-flat seat across the Pacific. Both halves are true, and guides that tell you only the first half are why people quit.


## Which Points Should You Earn First? Transferable Points vs Airline Miles


Transferable card points are the better starting point because they move into many airline programs, while airline miles lock you into one airline.


The difference is simple. Airline miles live with one airline and can only book that airline and its partners. *Transferable points* are card points that can be moved into a range of different airline programs, most of them at a 1:1 ratio ([NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/travel/learn/ranking-the-chase-transfer-partners) ). Five programs issue them: Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt.


At the earning stage that flexibility matters more than it ever will again, because you do not yet know which airline flies your trip at the best price. You may not even know the trip. Transferable points keep the decision open until a specific seat is in front of you. Earning airline miles first means picking the airline before you have picked the destination, which is the wrong order.


Two practical notes before you start. Most transfers are instant, though some Amex partners can take up to five days. Transfers cannot be reversed, so points move once you have found the seat, never in advance. The full mechanics live in our[guide to booking flights with credit card points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-book-flights-with-credit-card-points) .


## What Slows People Down: Five Honest Mistakes


Most beginners lose time by carrying a balance, splitting points across programs, hoarding them, waiting for a perfect redemption, or letting airline miles expire.


1. **Carrying a balance.** A card earning 2 points per dollar returns roughly two cents on the dollar. A revolving balance costs many times that. This one is not close.
2. **Spreading points across four programs.** Three balances of 20,000 book nothing. One balance of 60,000 books a trip. Concentrate until you have a bookable pile, then diversify if you want to.
3. **Hoarding.** Programs devalue their charts over time, and many have moved to dynamic pricing where the number of points needed is hard to forecast at all ([CFPB](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_credit-card-rewards_issue-spotlight_2024-05.pdf) ). Points are worth more today than they are likely to be worth later.
4. **Waiting for the perfect redemption.** The 4,500-point short-haul award is a real win and a good first booking. People pass on it for two years waiting for a business class seat they never end up booking.
5. **Earning airline miles for a trip you have not chosen.** Then finding that airline does not fly the route well, and the balance is stuck.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How many points do you need for a free flight?


As few as 4,500 points for a short domestic one-way, around 12,500 for Hawaii, and from roughly 6,000 to 40,000 for economy to Europe depending on the program and the date. Award prices move, so treat these as starting points rather than fixed rates.


### How long does it take to earn enough points for a flight?


It depends on how much you spend and whether you open a new card. Earning a welcome bonus compresses the timeline to a few months of ordinary spending, while everyday spending alone typically takes considerably longer. The scenario table above shows the assumptions behind each estimate.


### Can you earn enough points for a free flight without opening a new credit card?


Yes, but it takes longer. Everyday spending on a card you already hold still accumulates, and shopping portals, referral bonuses, and flying add to it. A welcome bonus is simply the fastest single deposit available.


### Are points and miles flights actually free?


Not entirely. The seat costs points instead of cash, but taxes and fees still apply, ranging from a few dollars on some programs to several hundred on others. "Free flight" is shorthand for an award flight.


### What is the fastest way to earn points for travel?


Meeting the minimum spending requirement on a card's welcome bonus, using spending you were already going to do. Chasing a bonus with spending you would not otherwise make cancels out the value of the bonus.


## Key Takeaways


- A free flight does not require six figures. One-way award flights start at 4,500 points on short domestic routes.
- Points arrive three ways: a welcome bonus, everyday spending, and smaller extras like shopping portals and referrals.
- The welcome bonus is the accelerator and everyday spending is the engine. Most people need both, because a bonus pays once per card.
- Timelines depend on your spending and your card. State your own assumptions before you trust any estimate, including the ones here.
- Transferable points beat airline miles at the earning stage, because they keep the destination decision open until you see a seat.
- Award flights still carry taxes and fees, and award prices change, so take a good redemption rather than waiting for a perfect one.


## The Barrier Was Never the Balance


For most people the thing standing between them and a first award flight is not the point balance. It is never having known what the trip costs, and therefore never having aimed at it. Once the target is a number, earning turns into arithmetic instead of a vague ambition.
